title: C++ OOP Deep Dive
description: Master advanced object-oriented mechanics in C++: Pure virtual functions, virtual destructors, object slicing, diamond problem with virtual inheritance, and dependency injection.

topics.title: Abstract Classes & Pure Virtual Functions
topics.description: Defining immutable API contracts with pure virtual functions (= 0) and interface segregation in C++.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: An Abstract Class is a class containing at least one Pure Virtual Function (syntax: virtual void method() = 0;). It defines an interface specification that cannot be instantiated directly.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: In large systems, modules must interact via stable behavioral contracts without binding to concrete subsystem implementations. Abstract classes enforce that derived classes implement required operations at compile time.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: A pure virtual function acts as an obligatory checklist for subclasses. If a subclass fails to override even one pure virtual function, that subclass also becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: The compiler sets the VTable entry for pure virtual functions to a null pointer or standard trap function (__cxa_pure_virtual). A derived class overrides this entry with its own function pointer.

Lines 6-11: ILogger has pure virtual functions = 0.
Line 14: Pure virtual destructors must have an out-of-line body (inline ILogger::~ILogger() = default;) because derived destructors implicitly invoke the base destructor during cleanup.
Lines 32-37: Demonstrates hot-swapping logger implementations seamlessly via std::unique_ptr<ILogger>.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Operating system HALs (Hardware Abstraction Layers), graphics rendering APIs (Vulkan vs DirectX vs Metal), and cloud telemetry exporters.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use abstract classes whenever you want to define a strict API contract that multiple pluggable subclasses must fulfill.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use abstract interfaces for concrete internal domain objects that have no polymorphic variations.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content:
• Compile-time verification of subclass completeness.
  • Zero-coupling dependency injection.
  • Clean mock injection for unit tests.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Virtual function dispatch overhead ($O(1)$ VTable indirection).

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Pure Interfaces (no member variables), Abstract Base Classes with shared state and helper methods.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Declaring a pure virtual destructor without providing a definition body, causing an unresolved external symbol linker error at runtime.

callout.title: Pure Virtual Destructor Linker Trap
callout.text: Even if declared `virtual ~Base() = 0;`, you MUST provide a definition `Base::~Base() {}`. Destructors are always invoked in reverse hierarchy order during derived cleanup!

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Can a pure virtual function have an implementation body in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Yes! In C++, a pure virtual function can have a body defined outside the class (e.g. void IBase::commonLogic() { ... }). Derived classes must still explicitly override it, but they can choose to call the base implementation via IBase::commonLogic().

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Design an IAuthenticator interface with pure virtual authenticate(username, password) and implement OAuthAuthenticator and LdapAuthenticator.

practice.title: Pluggable Authenticator Interface
practice.problemStatement: Build an authentication abstraction supporting OAuth and LDAP backends.
requirements: pure virtual bool authenticate(string u, string p) = 0

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Abstract classes and pure virtual functions are the foundation of decoupled, extensible, and clean Low-Level System Design in C++.

topics.title: Virtual Destructors & Polymorphic Deletion
topics.description: Why base classes with virtual functions must have virtual destructors to prevent fatal undefined behavior and memory leaks.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Virtual Destructor is a destructor declared with the virtual keyword in a base class (virtual ~Base() = default;) to guarantee that when a derived object is deleted through a base class pointer, the complete destructor chain executes in reverse hierarchy order.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Deleting a derived object via a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is Undefined Behavior (UB) according to the C++ Standard [§8.3.5]. The derived destructor is bypassed entirely, causing catastrophic memory leaks and unreleased OS resources.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: 'If a class has at least ONE virtual function, its destructor MUST be virtual.'

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: When the destructor is virtual, its address is placed into the class's VTable. Calling delete basePtr; looks up the destructor dynamically, executing the derived destructor first, followed by base destructors.

sections.content: Line 5: virtual ~BaseClean() ensures delete polyPtr executes DerivedResource::~DerivedResource() before BaseClean::~BaseClean(), freeing the 1000-int heap buffer.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Factory patterns creating plugins, UI controls, or database connections that are returned as std::unique_ptr<IBase>.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always declare base class destructors virtual if the class is designed for polymorphic inheritance.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not make destructors virtual for non-polymorphic value classes (like std::vector, std::string, or small math structs) because it injects an unnecessary 8-byte VPTR.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Guarantees complete resource reclamation and prevents undefined behavior.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: 8-byte VPTR overhead if the class had no other virtual functions.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: virtual ~Base() = default; (Preferred), protected ~Base() = default; (Disallows polymorphic deletion through base pointer).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Inheriting publicly from standard library containers (like std::vector) which have non-virtual destructors!

callout.title: Inheriting from std::vector Trap
callout.text: class MyVector : public std::vector<int> { ... }; std::vector<int>* ptr = new MyVector(); delete ptr; // CATASTROPHIC UB: std::vector has no virtual destructor!

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: If a base class destructor is protected and non-virtual, what architectural constraint does it enforce?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A protected non-virtual destructor prevents callers from calling delete basePtr; (causing a compile-time error). It enforces that derived objects must be managed and deleted only through derived pointers, eliminating polymorphic deletion risks without paying for an 8-byte VPTR.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Create a PluginBase class and verify that derived plugins clean up custom OS threads on destruction.

practice.title: Plugin Cleanup Verification
practice.problemStatement: Implement PluginBase with virtual destructor to ensure thread shutdown.
requirements: Derived plugin thread shutdown in destructor

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Virtual destructors are a mandatory rule for polymorphic base classes in modern C++ Low-Level Design.

topics.title: Object Slicing & Value Semantics Trap
topics.description: Understanding object slicing when passing polymorphic objects by value, and how to defend against it.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Object Slicing occurs when a derived class object is assigned or passed by value to a base class object (Base b = derivedObj;). The derived portions (extra member variables and derived VTable) are literally sliced off, leaving only the base sub-object.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Understanding object slicing is critical to avoid catastrophic bugs where polymorphism silently breaks because an object was passed by value instead of by reference/pointer.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Always pass polymorphic objects by reference (const Base&) or smart pointer (std::unique_ptr<Base>), NEVER by value.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: A Base object's memory is only large enough for Base's members. When assigning a Derived object to a Base value, the copy constructor of Base executes, copying only the base fields and resetting the vptr to the Base VTable.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Slicing Diagram in Memory:

callout.title: Memory Slicing Anatomy
callout.text: Derived Object: [Base Part: id, vptr_Derived] + [Derived Part: extraBuffer, customId]\nPass By Value: Base b = derived; -> Copies ONLY [Base Part: id, vptr_BASE] -> [Derived Part] is discarded!

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Line 21: void drawWindowSlices(Window w) slices the modal dialog into a plain Window.
Line 26: void drawWindowCorrect(const Window& w) preserves the full ModalDialog instance in memory.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Storing polymorphic objects inside standard containers: std::vector<Base> slices objects; use std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>> instead.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use value semantics for non-polymorphic Value Objects (e.g. Money, Point2D). Use reference semantics for polymorphic class hierarchies.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Never store polymorphic derived instances in a by-value base container (e.g. std::vector<Animal>).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Understanding slicing prevents silent logic bugs where overrides fail to execute.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Slicing is a C++ language quirk that does not produce a compile-time error by default.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Slicing during assignment (b = d;), Slicing during pass-by-value, Slicing during vector push_back.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Catching polymorphic exceptions by value (catch (std::exception ex) slices derived exception data; always write catch (const std::exception& ex)!).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How can you make a polymorphic base class completely immune to object slicing at compile time?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Make the base class Abstract (at least one pure virtual function = 0) or delete/protect its copy constructor (Base(const Base&) = delete;). This causes the compiler to reject any attempt to instantiate or copy a Base object by value, eliminating slicing at compile time.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor a sliced std::vector<Employee> container into a memory-safe polymorphic std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Employee>> container.

practice.title: Eliminating Vector Slicing
practice.problemStatement: Fix vector slicing by switching to unique_ptr storage.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Defend against object slicing by passing polymorphic objects via references or smart pointers and making base classes abstract.

topics.title: Diamond Problem & Virtual Inheritance
topics.description: Resolving multiple inheritance ambiguity and duplicate base class instances using virtual base classes.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Diamond Problem occurs in multiple inheritance when a class derives from two classes that both inherit from a common base class. Without Virtual Inheritance, the most-derived class receives two duplicate copies of the common base class, creating ambiguity and wasted memory.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: In real-world architectures (like the standard C++ I/O stream hierarchy where std::iostream inherits from both std::istream and std::ostream, which both inherit from std::ios_base), duplicate base sub-objects corrupt shared state. Virtual inheritance guarantees exactly ONE shared base instance.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Use virtual public Base during intermediate inheritance: class B : virtual public A. This tells the compiler that class A is a shared virtual base.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: The compiler injects a Virtual Base Table Pointer (VBTR). The most-derived class becomes directly responsible for constructing the shared virtual base class, bypassing intermediate constructors.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: The standard library std::iostream (inheriting virtually from std::basic_ios).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use virtual inheritance when designing diamond class hierarchies that share common base state.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Avoid multiple inheritance with state altogether when composition or interface realization can be used instead.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates ambiguity and avoids duplicate base memory allocation.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Slight memory indirection overhead via virtual base pointer (VBTR); constructor delegation rules become complex.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Virtual Public, Virtual Protected, Virtual Private inheritance.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to initialize the virtual base class from the most-derived constructor, leading to the default constructor being called unexpectedly.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Who is responsible for calling the constructor of a virtual base class in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: In virtual inheritance, the most-derived class is directly responsible for invoking the constructor of the virtual base class. Intermediate classes' calls to the virtual base constructor are ignored during most-derived object instantiation.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Model a PoweredDevice, BatteryPowered, SolarPowered, and HybridSolarCar hierarchy with virtual inheritance.

practice.title: Hybrid Solar Car Virtual Inheritance
practice.problemStatement: Build a hybrid car hierarchy using virtual inheritance.
practice.hint: Use virtual public PoweredDevice in intermediate classes.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Virtual inheritance solves the Diamond Problem by ensuring exactly one shared instance of a base class exists in the most-derived object.

topics.title: Composition vs Inheritance in C++
topics.description: Architectural trade-offs: Why composition provides loose coupling, dynamic flexibility, and avoids brittle base class hierarchies.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Inheritance ('is-a') creates a compile-time static binding between a subclass and a base class. Composition ('has-a') builds complex systems by assembling independent component objects together at runtime.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Overusing inheritance leads to the Brittle Base Class Problem: altering one base class method inadvertently breaks subclasses across the codebase. Composition keeps classes decoupled and easily testable.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: 'Favor object composition over class inheritance.' Use inheritance ONLY for polymorphic interface contracts; use composition for code reuse and behavioral assembly.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Instead of subclassing class CustomSet : public std::vector, compose the vector as a private member: class CustomSet { std::vector<int> elements; }; and delegate only the necessary operations.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation

rows: Exposes protected base state to subclasses

sections.content: Refactoring Brittle Inheritance into Flexible Composition:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Line 23: std::unique_ptr<IEngine> engine; embeds the behavioral strategy.
Line 30: setEngine() allows swapping propulsion algorithms at runtime—an impossibility with static class inheritance!

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Game entity component systems (ECS in Unity/Unreal), web server middleware pipelines, and customizable e-commerce pricing engines.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use composition whenever you need code reuse, dynamic component swapping, or loose coupling between subsystems.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Use inheritance only when there is a genuine polymorphic 'is-a' subtype relationship requiring Liskov substitution.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates class hierarchy explosion; allows dynamic behavior swapping; simplifies unit tests.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires writing forwarding/delegation methods.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Value Composition, Dynamic Strategy Composition (via interfaces), Delegation.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Inheriting from a class just to reuse one helper method (violates Liskov Substitution Principle).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why does composition adhere better to the Open/Closed Principle than inheritance?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: With composition and interface pointers, new behaviors are added by writing new component classes and injecting them, requiring ZERO changes to the container class. With inheritance, modifying a base class affects all derived subclasses, risking regression bugs.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor an inheritance-based Bird -> FlyingBird / NonFlyingBird hierarchy into a composed Bird with an injectable IFlyingBehavior.

refactor.title: Refactoring Brittle Bird Hierarchy to Strategy Composition
refactor.problemSummary: Inheritance forces all birds to inherit fly() methods, breaking Penguins and Ostriches.
violations: LSP violation when Penguin inherits fly()
benefits: Penguins can swim, Eagles can soar

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Favoring composition over inheritance is the single most important design guideline for maintainable, decoupled object-oriented systems.

topics.title: Dependency Injection & Delegation Idioms
topics.description: Constructor injection, interface delegation, inversion of control, and testable C++ architecture.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Dependency Injection (DI) is a technique where an object receives its dependencies from an external assembler rather than constructing them internally using new. Delegation is passing a method call directly to an internal helper object.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Hardcoding new MySQLDatabase() inside a service makes unit testing impossible without running a live database. Dependency Injection allows passing mock objects effortlessly.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Objects should not know how to construct their dependencies; they should only declare what interfaces they require to perform their jobs.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Dependencies are passed via Constructor Injection (preferred) or Setter Injection as std::shared_ptr<IInterface> or std::unique_ptr<IInterface>.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Dependency Injection Flow:

callout.title: Inversion of Control (IoC)
callout.text: Traditional: Service -> creates -> ConcreteDatabase (High coupling)\nDependency Injection: Main/Assembler -> injects -> Interface -> Service (Decoupled)

sections.content:
Lines 30-34: UserService requires an INotificationGateway in its constructor.
Lines 47-52: In unit tests, a lightweight mock is injected with zero network calls, verifying behavior instantly.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Enterprise microservices, gRPC service handlers, and financial order processing systems.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always use Constructor Dependency Injection for external services, data storage, and network dependencies.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not inject primitive data structures (like std::vector or std::string) or trivial value objects.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: 100% testability; satisfies SOLID Dependency Inversion Principle; enables modular deployment.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Slight increase in constructor parameter boilerplate.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Constructor Injection, Setter Injection, Interface Injection, Dependency Injection Containers.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Using the Service Locator anti-pattern (a global registry that hides true dependencies) instead of explicit Constructor Injection.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is Constructor Injection preferred over Setter Injection in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Constructor Injection guarantees that the object is fully initialized and immutable with all required dependencies from the moment of construction. Setter Injection allows the object to exist in an incomplete, uninitialized state where calling methods before the setter triggers null pointer crashes.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem

practice.title: Multi-Dependency Constructor Injection
practice.problemStatement: Build OrderProcessor taking payment gateway and inventory dependencies.
practice.hint: Store both as shared_ptr interface members.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Dependency Injection decouples high-level policy from low-level execution, enabling testable and production-ready object-oriented systems.
